# Report: “Inflationary Paradigm after Planck 2013” (Guth, Kaiser, Nomura)

**1. The question, frozen**

Several questions are answered here (what Planck constrains; whether the Higgs story bites inflation). The one the title and opening make central: *Is the inflationary paradigm — early accelerated expansion that explains today’s observable features — still on firm footing after Planck 2013, i.e. are Ijjas–Steinhardt–Loeb (ISL) right that it is in trouble?* Range: the observable universe, from the last ~60 e-folds to today, judged against CMB and LHC data. Kind: an argument (does the defence achieve its purpose?). I hold this fixed; the other questions are treated below as jobs.

**2. The explanation, in parts**

Its claim: inflation’s inflation-scale predictions match Planck, and each ISL criticism rests on one replaceable assumption — mainly that a single uninterrupted inflation ran from the Planck scale to now.

**3. Part by part**

Jobs, and where each came from: **J1** predictions match Planck (given). **J2** successful plateau models are exponentially unlikely from Planck-scale assumptions (given, ISL). **J3** the plateau-vs-power-law “unlikeliness problem” (given, ISL). **J4** multiverse unpredictability (given, ISL). **J5** the Higgs potential turns negative (given, ISL). **J6** a Hubble-sized homogeneous region needs only ~1–15 Hubble lengths at the Planck scale (added). **J7** observables are independent of pre-inflation physics (added).

| Part | Mark |
|---|---|
| Inflation-scale predictions (flatness, red tilt, Gaussian, coherent peaks) | **Held** — by J1 (flip the tilt sign or raise r and Planck would disagree) |
| Slow-roll attractor: observables independent of what came before | **Held** — by slow-roll dynamics; the strongest part, and the one doing the real work |
| Getting a homogeneous Planck-scale region without tuning | **Held if** — by the added job J6; and **Two routes** do it (open k<0 scaling ∝t, *or* tunneling from a metastable state) |
| The “13.9” worst-case number | **Held** — by the FRW + a∝t calculation; but its a∝t assumption and the causality theorem are **Borrowed** (Wald) |
| V(φ) complicated, many minima (string theory) | **Held if** — by the added job “start inflation without tuning”; nothing observational holds it. Would be settled by evidence for a landscape: none |
| Tunneling before the last inflation (φ̇=0, homogeneous) | **Held if** — same added job; a neighbour does as well, so **Two routes** with the k<0 entry |
| Eternal inflation / multiverse | **Held if** — by the job “the plateau is real”; out of doubt otherwise |
| “Acceptable measures exist” (proper-time ruled out; scale-factor cutoff) | **Borrowed** (Refs 16–20) and **Loose** — any of several would do, and the paper cannot compute which dominates |
| Anthropic selection (N≳59.5) | **Borrowed** — from the vacuum-energy anthropic argument |
| Enhanced-symmetry point / multi-field settling | **Loose** — a constructed toy; several would do |
| Higgs negative region cannot host life | **Borrowed** — rests on GR + SM assumptions |
| “Cyclic models have a measure problem too” | **Idle** — removing it loses no job for the central claim |
| The “inflationary paradigm = yes to both questions” definition | **Fixed** — the authors set it; not tested |
| Whether new physics exists below the Higgs turnaround scale | **Unknown** — would be settled by discovering (or ruling out) SUSY at accessible scales |

**4. Whole-explanation checks**

*Flip.* Had Planck favoured a power-law potential (large r), the framework would have worked too: the paper says plateau and power-law are both “perfectly consistent” and it cannot say which is likelier. So the defence covers either outcome; only the inflation-scale predictions can be caught.

*Direction.* J1 runs forward (theory → observables), which is right. The “unlikeliness” rebuttal runs backward from the observed plateau — fine for “what can we tell”, not for “what produces it.”

*Answer in the starting points.* Defining the paradigm as “yes, both” is a definition (allowed). But the multiverse-plus-anthropic layer makes “we see a universe like ours” nearly automatic and so hard to catch — the mirror of ISL’s “describes the data too well” charge, which the paper notes but does not fully answer.

*Pull.* A potential complicated enough to give many minima loosens the low-energy plateau’s shape — the paper concedes “inflation does not determine the shape.” Predictivity gives way to eternal inflation; the paper rescues predictivity with the attractor part (held). Name that pair.

*Catch-alls and gauges.* “Some acceptable measure” has a gauge — the youngness problem (proper-time cutoff predicts T<3K absurdly improbably). “Complicated V” has a partial gauge — Planck still forces the plateau and r<0.12. “Anthropic selection” has a stated gauge (observers must be possible) but it is not computable.

*Change list, and what it leaves out.* The paper openly sets Planck-scale physics aside as beyond test — an honest, free limit. It leaves out any observational handle on the pre-inflation phase (no-hair); that is exactly why J7 works.

*Rivals.* ISL’s single-phase fine-tuning story differs from this one only over unobservable pre-inflation history. No change on the list tells them apart at the level of CMB observables — **at this level they are the same explanation.** The real dispute is over the added assumption in J3, which the paper says is not computable today.

*Where the parts came from.* The inflation-scale predictions and the attractor are **built** (they commit to numbers and can be caught). The complicated-V, tunneling and measure parts are **fitted or asserted** (chosen so the framework survives). The measure and Higgs parts are **borrowed**.

**5. What would make it harder to vary**

(a) Commit. Either defend a plateau-vs-power-law probability under a named measure, or say plainly it is unknowable and drop the claim that ISL’s probability is wrong. It does both, which loosens that part.

(b) Give the “complicated V” part a gauge — name an observation that would show V is featureless after all, e.g. a bubble-collision non-Gaussianity. Then it could be caught, not just asserted.

**6. What this does not show**

Hard to vary is not true. Passing means the inflation-scale predictions stick their neck out and can be caught; the defensive layer around them does not. It says nothing about whether inflation is correct.

**7. One next step**

Before more data, write down the one or two observations that would break the defence (r above ~0.12, a blue tilt, or bubble-collision non-Gaussianity) and, for each, name which part it refutes.
